union.text: northern Burma to Tagaung, the province of Zhengmian (Pagan's 1285 shape north of 23.5 N; the mongol-empire dossier's ledger/86 region)

land.text: China, Mongolia and the east under Kublai's line, with the province of Zhengmian (northern Burma to Tagaung, mongol-empire ledger/86)

predecessors.note: 'Khagan-ruled division of the Mongol Empire' (P1 infobox). The Yuan name dates from 1271 and the conquest of the Song from 1279 (P1); Cliopatria keeps both inside its Mongol Empire row to 1293 and starts a Yuan row in 1294, and the mongol-empire dossier carries the rename of 1271 and the conquests. This dossier starts where the shapes do.

land.text: the Yuan land the Ming take in 1369: Taiyuan and Shanxi (January 1369), Shaanxi (by September 1369) (Hongwu Emperor page); the Ming ledger dates every later gain itself (Shangdu and the Inner Mongolia margin 1369-70, Sichuan September 1371, Gansu 1372, Yunnan 1381-82, Manchuria 1387-88)

successors.note: Zhu Yuanzhang proclaimed the Ming on 12 January 1368 (P2); the Cliopatria Ming row begins in 1375. fx-38 (H12): the land was Cliopatria's Ming 1375 shape, which gave the Ming at the dissolve about 7,860 cells (Inner Mongolia, Gansu, Liaoning, Jilin, Guizhou, Ningxia) that were Ming only from 1370 to 1388. Hongwu Emperor page: 'The main army, led by Xu Da, captured Taiyuan in January 1369'; 'They had fully captured the province [Shaanxi] by September 1369'; 'By September 1371, Sichuan had been conquered'; 'the Ming army, led by Fu Youde, quickly conquered Yunnan' (1381-1382); 'The campaign into Manchuria in 1387 was ultimately successful'.

land.text: the Mongolian Plateau, where the Genghisid court retreated in 1368 (P1)
Yunnan, where the Prince of Liang Basalawarmi held out until 1381 (P1)
Ü-Tsang, central Tibet, superseded from Sakya rule in 1354-1358 (P4)

successors.note: Not Yuan-held land at the end: the Sakya regime's vassal land passed to the Phagmodrupa in 1354-1358 (P4) and the vassal tint ended in 1358 (ledger). Listed because P1 names the Phagmodrupa dynasty among the Yuan's successors.

capitals.name: Dadu (Khanbaliq; Beijing)
capitals.note: P1: 'Dadu (now Beijing), with Shangdu as summer capital'; Kaiping was 'later renamed Shangdu' (about 116.18 E, 42.36 N, Inner Mongolia). P1 gives no year for the move to Dadu; the mongol-empire dossier has 1271. Toghon Temür left Dadu in September 1368.

rulers.name: Shizu (Kublai)
rulers.note: Khagan from 1260 (P1); the Zhiyuan era ends 18 February 1294 (P3), the day Kublai died (P1).

rulers.name: Chengzong (Temür Khan)
rulers.note: P1: 'ruled as Temür Khan, or Emperor Chengzong, from 1294 to 1307'; the Dade era ends 10 February 1307 (P3).

rulers.name: Wuzong (Qaishan, Külüg Khan)
rulers.note: P1: 'During his short reign (1307-11)'; the Zhida era runs 23 January 1308 - 27 January 1311 (P3).

rulers.name: Renzong (Ayurbarwada, Buyantu Khan)
rulers.note: Huangqing and Yanyou eras, 7 April 1311 - 1 March 1320 (P3).

rulers.name: Taiding Emperor (Yesün Temür)
rulers.note: Taiding era from 3 January 1324; the Zhihe era ends 15 August 1328 (P3); P1: he 'died in Shangdu in 1328'. The start in 1323 follows the 4 September 1323 end of the previous reign and the page's reign length of 4 years, 10 months.

rulers.name: Tianshun Emperor (Ragibagh)
rulers.title: child emperor
rulers.note: October - 14 November 1328 (P3), the Shangdu side of the War of the Two Capitals (P1); the name Ragibagh is P1's.

rulers.name: Wenzong (Tugh Temür), first reign
rulers.note: 16 October 1328 - 26 February 1329 (P3); abdicated for his brother.

rulers.name: Mingzong (Kusala)
rulers.note: 27 February - 30 August 1329 (P3); 'suddenly died only four days after a banquet with Tugh Temür' (P1).

rulers.name: Wenzong (Tugh Temür), second reign
rulers.note: P3 gives 2 years, 11 months and 25 days to 2 September 1332; P1 'the death of Tugh Temür in 1332'.

rulers.name: Ningzong (Irinjibal)
rulers.title: child emperor
rulers.note: 23 October - 14 December 1332 (P3); the name Rinchinbal is P1's.

rulers.name: Huizong (Toghon Temür)
rulers.note: P3: Yuantong era from 15 November 1333, Zhizheng era ends 10 September 1368; P1 infobox gives 1332-1368. Flees Dadu in September 1368; dies at Yingchang on 23 May 1370 (P2).

minus.text: Kaidu and Duwa's Uighuria and Beshbalik, and the Tarim Basin

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1294 Yuan shape without the Goryeo kingdom (a 'Mongol tributary state') and without Ü-Tsang (the Sakya lamas' government under the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs), plus the province of Zhengmian (northern Burma to Tagaung), which the Yuan held from the mongol-empire handover until 4 April 1303 and Cliopatria's Yuan shape leaves out; valid 1294-1351 (Zhengmian to the ledger's loss of April 1303); also without the Tarim Basin and the Ögedeid lands (Uighuria, Beshbalik): the Yuan had begun to leave Kashgar, Khotan and Beshbalik in 1288/89 and Kaidu and Duwa held Beshbaliq from 1286 (fx-26)

keyframe_review.note: 14.25 M km2 for 1294-1351. P1's infobox gives 11.0 M km2 for 1310 (ratio 0.77 of the shape); the corrected shape is 13.3 M km2 (0.83), within a factor of two, so the extent is accepted: all China (Yunnan 92 percent), Mongolia, Manchuria, 35 percent of Xinjiang, a quarter of Russia up to 61.5 N. P1 names 'areas of Lingbei province' (Henning Circuit, Yilan, Qian Prefecture) for Han officials in the north and colonists at Besh Baliq, Almaliq and Samarqand but no Tarim claim; the north and the Xinjiang edge are unverified (page budget). Korea (0.19 M km2 as goryeo draws it) and Ü-Tsang (0.77 M km2) are removed and become vassal tints (ledger 1294). Hamgyong stays Yuan until 1356, and Jeju, Tamna Prefecture to 1294-1301 per the goryeo dossier, is not cut. Zhengmian, northern Burma to Tagaung (about 0.065 M km2 by the gazetteer, 256 cells), is added from the mongol-empire dossier (ledger/86, 1284, citing the First Mongol invasion of Burma page): Cliopatria's Yuan shape holds 0.4 percent of Myanmar and none of it. The ledger takes it out on 4 April 1303; the areas and ratios above change by less than 0.5 percent. [fx-26, F193/F191: Cliopatria's shape draws 2,018 cells (35 percent) of Xinjiang as Yuan land. Kaidu page: 'Kaidu and Duwa were able to take over Beshbaliq in 1286, forcing Kublai's troops to evacuate Uighuria'; Kaidu-Kublai war page: 'the Yuan was forced to start withdrawing from Kashgar, Khotan and Beshbalik' in 1288/89. 749 cells of the shape lay inside the Ogedeid ulus of 1289-1306 (613 cell-years given to the Ogedeid at 1294 by the size rule), 633 of them Qocho's, a Yuan vassal inside the Yuan by hierarchy.csv; the Tarim Basin has no page for Yuan rule after 1289. About 360 Xinjiang cells (6 percent) are left, unverified.]

minus.text: Kaidu and Duwa's Uighuria and Beshbalik, the Tarim Basin and the Kingdom of Qocho

correction.text: the same corrected shape as 1294, as the state at the start of 1352; the ledger takes the rebel and Korean and Tibetan land out year by year, to the 1363 shape. Zhengmian is NOT added back here: it was given up on 4 April 1303 (ledger), nine years before 1352, so the 1352 start state does not hold it; also without the Tarim Basin, the Ögedeid lands and the Kingdom of Qocho (fx-26)

keyframe_review.note: 14.25 M km2, identical to 1294 within 0.01 percent: Cliopatria draws no loss in the first eleven years of the Red Turban Rebellions (1351-1362), although P2 dates the Tianwan at Qishui (September 1351), Zhang Shicheng at Gaoyou (end of 1353), Zhu Yuanzhang at Nanjing (10 April 1356), Chen Youliang's Han (1360), and the Song loyalists at Bozhou (16 March 1355). The shape is right at 1352 and wrong from 1353; the ledger carries the losses 1351-1363, and the rendering applies them to this shape. Disagreement with the reviewer's fix 2 (add Zhengmian to the 1352 correction as well): the Yuan abolished Zhengmian and left Tagaung on 4 April 1303 (First Mongol invasion of Burma page), so a 1352 shape that held it would draw the province again forty-nine years after it was lost. [fx-26, F191: Qocho's land (633 cells) was drawn again as direct Yuan land at 1352, after the Mongol vassalage ended in 1335 (Kingdom of Qocho page: 'Vassal state of the Mongol Empire (1209-1335)'); Qocho goes on to 1352 and the 1370s as a state of its own, 'allied with the Yuan against the Chagatai Khanate', then 'part of the Chagatai Khanate' (no year). Taken out with the Tarim and Ogedeid lands, as in 1294.]

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1363 Yuan shape (already without Korea and central Tibet) minus the provinces in rebel hands by 1363 (Jiangsu, Shanghai, Zhejiang, Anhui, Jiangxi, Hubei, Hunan, Sichuan, Chongqing), except the Bozhou-Yingzhou district of western Anhui, which the Yuan retook in 1359 and kept (ledger 1359), and minus Quanzhou and Putian, held by the Ispah army from 1357 and returned to the Yuan in 1366 (ledger); valid 1363-1368; also without the Tarim Basin, Uighuria and the Kingdom of Qocho (fx-26)

keyframe_review.note: 12.2 M km2 for 1363-1374; the corrected 1363-1367 shape is 10.9 M km2 (P1's 11.0 M km2 is for 1310; no infobox figure is near 1363). The shape correctly drops Korea and Xizang by 1363 (ledger 1356 and 1358) but still draws all of south China, where P2 has the Tianwan and Han, Zhang Shicheng's Wu, Zhu Yuanzhang's Wu, Fang Guozhen and Ming Yuzhen in 1363. The cut is by whole province, an approximation: parts of Hubei and Hunan may still have been Yuan-held, and no page opened says. Repaired 2026-10-25: the two Bozhou-Yingzhou circles (ledger 1359 retaking, no later loss on any page opened; the Red Turban page is silent on Yuan control of Anhui after 1359) stay Yuan to 1368, and Quanzhou and Putian are cut for 1363-1365 (Ispah rebellion, 1357-1366) and come back with the 1366 gain. The shape stops at the fall of Dadu in September 1368: Cliopatria runs it to 1374 over land that was Ming (China) or Northern Yuan (Mongolia, the northern-yuan dossier) by then, so 1369-1374 is not drawn from it. Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, Shandong and Henan remain Yuan to 1368; no page opened dates the Ming conquest of Fujian, Guangdong or Guangxi (unverified: page budget). The Cliopatria Xinjiang edge (35 to 20 percent in 1363) and the loss of south-west Qinghai and west Sichuan are not explained by any page opened (the tibet dossier takes Ü-Tsang only); unverified: page budget. [fx-26, F191: same as 1352: Qocho's land (542 cells in this shape), the Tarim Basin and Uighuria are not direct Yuan land.]

union.text: northern Burma to Tagaung, the province of Zhengmian (Pagan's 1285 shape north of 23.5 N; the mongol-empire dossier's ledger/86 region)
the Ögedeid ulus of 1289-1306: Semirechye, Almaliq, Bukhara, Beshbalik and Uighuria (Turfan-Hami)
the Tarim Basin, evacuated by the Yuan from 1288/89

minus.text: Kaidu and Duwa's Uighuria and Beshbalik, and the Tarim Basin

region.text: China, Mongolia, Manchuria, the eastern steppe and the province of Zhengmian (northern Burma to Tagaung) under Kublai's line: Cliopatria's 1294 Yuan shape without the Goryeo kingdom and without Ü-Tsang, which the Yuan ruled through client governments, plus Zhengmian, which Cliopatria leaves out; without the Tarim Basin and the Ögedeid lands of Uighuria and Beshbalik

ledger.note: 1294: Kublai dies on 18 February and Temür Khan succeeds him; the Yuan stands as the eastern khanate among the four successors of the Mongol Empire. The page says the dynasty 'lasted from 1271 to 1368' and that 'it was not until 1271 that Kublai Khan officially proclaimed the dynasty in the traditional Han style' (5 November 1271), with the conquest complete in 1279 at Yamen; that earlier history (rename 1271, Song conquest 1276-1279) is in the mongol-empire dossier, which hands its land to this one in 1294, as Cliopatria does (Yuan row from 1294). Temür Khan 'ruled ... from 1294 to 1307'. Month 2 is Kublai's death (P1), not a founding month. Repaired 2026-10-25: the region adds Zhengmian, northern Burma to Tagaung, which the mongol-empire dossier (ledger/86, 1284) holds and hands over in 1293 (First Mongol invasion of Burma page: 'The Mongols continued to occupy northern Burma to Tagaung as the province of Zhengmian'). [fx-26, F193: region cut like keyframe yuan-dynasty_1294 (Tarim Basin and the Ögedeid lands out; Kaidu page and Kaidu-Kublai war page).]

region.text: the Kingdom of Goryeo as the goryeo dossier draws it for 1290-1355: the Cliopatria 1227 outline plus North Pyongan up to the Yalu

ledger.note: Goryeo is a Yuan tributary throughout the dossier's first six decades. 'In 1259 Kublai installed Wonjong as the ruler of the Kingdom of Goryeo', making it 'a Mongol tributary state' and betrothing a daughter to the prince (P1). The relation began in 1259 (the mongol-empire dossier holds that vassal_start); this event only carries it into 1294. Cliopatria draws all of Korea as direct Yuan land from 1260 to 1362 (South Korea 99 percent, North Korea 99.6 percent of the cells in the shape); the corrected shape removes the Goryeo kingdom and draws it as a vassal tint.

region.text: Ü-Tsang, central Tibet, as the tibet and sakya-regime dossiers draw it: the gazetteer's Central Tibet without Chamdo (Kham) and without the Guge, Latö and Mangyül Gungthang circles

ledger.note: Tibet under the Sakya lamas as the Yuan's client government. The Phagmodrupa page: 'The Sakya regime, centered in Tsang (West Central Tibet) had hitherto wielded power over Tibet on behalf of the Mongols' and the Yuan was 'overlord of Tibet'; the Yuan page adds that the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs 'governed Tibet' and that 14 Sakya leaders held the post of Imperial Preceptor. Neither page dates the start, which the sakya-regime dossier puts at 1264, so 1294 is only this dossier's first year (confidence 1). Cliopatria draws Xizang (99 percent of the cells) as direct Yuan land to 1362; the corrected shape removes Ü-Tsang. The Yuan page's wording ('governed') also fits a province; the tint is a judgement, see notes.

region.text: the Altai and western Mongolia between Karakorum and the Dzungarian steppe (the ogedeid-ulus dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1294 (bookkeeping): the fight with Kaidu's House of Ogedei over the Altai and western Mongolia passes from the mongol-empire row to this one; the ogedeid-ulus dossier dates its contest to 1289. The Kaidu-Kublai war page dates no campaign in 1294 (1293: Tutugh occupies the Baarin tumen; 1298: Duwa attacks a Yuan garrison in Mongolia; 1300: Kaidu defeats Khayishan's force) and does not name western Mongolia; the zone is the other dossier's reading.

region.text: northern Sakhalin, where the Northern Sakhalin Ainu fought the Mongols (the ainu dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1294 (bookkeeping): the Mongol war with the Sakhalin Ainu (30 November 1264 to 1308, infobox) passes from the mongol-empire row to this one. The page dates no campaign in 1294-1296 (an Ainu raid on the mainland was beaten near Lake Kizi in mid-1297) and does not say the Yuan held northern Sakhalin; the zone is the ainu dossier's reading of the Ainu land the Mongols pressed.

region.text: Singu and Male, the southernmost Mongol garrisons, about 70 km from Tagaung (the myinsaing-kingdom dossier's circle)

ledger.note: January 1300: Athinkhaya's army 'seized lightly manned southernmost Mongol garrisons' at Singu and Male, about 70 km from Tagaung. The Yuan backed Kumara Kassapa and sent the second Mongol invasion (1300-01): it 'managed to reach Myinsaing on 25 January 1301' and was called off for a bribe on 6 April 1301. The circle is the myinsaing-kingdom dossier's; Singu and Male lie just south of the Zhengmian box.

region.text: the Altai and western Mongolia between Karakorum and the Dzungarian steppe (the ogedeid-ulus dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1301: Kaidu dies after the battle near Karakorum and the House of Ogedei's war on the Yuan ends (infobox 1268-1301, inconclusive). 'Kaidu died in 1301 after the battle near Karakorum'; Duwa, wounded in it, made peace with the Yuan in 1304 (see the war entry).

region.text: Singu and Male, the southernmost Mongol garrisons, about 70 km from Tagaung (the myinsaing-kingdom dossier's circle)

ledger.note: 4 April 1303: the Mongols 'withdrew from northern Burma entirely on 4 April 1303' (Myinsaing page; infobox 'Mongol evacuation: 4 April 1303').

region.text: northern Burma to Tagaung, the province of Zhengmian (Pagan's 1285 shape north of 23.5 N; the mongol-empire dossier's ledger/86 region)

ledger.note: 4 April 1303: the Yuan abolish the province of Zhengmian, evacuate Tagaung and return to Yunnan. 'on 4 April 1303, the Mongols abolished the province of Zhengmian (Cheng-Mien)'. The page names no successor, so the land goes to nobody; the Myinsaing page adds, undated and after the withdrawal, that the brothers 'took over Tagaung but could not go any farther north' because Shan states held the arc around the Irrawaddy valley, so the town of Tagaung on the southern edge of the box may have passed to myinsaing-kingdom (confidence 2: date and loss are the page's, the counterpart is a reading). The Myinsaing dossier's 1303 gain of the Dry Zone (Kyaukse, Minbu, Mu) is not Zhengmian land and the page does not say the Yuan held it.

region.text: northern Sakhalin, where the Northern Sakhalin Ainu fought the Mongols (the ainu dossier's zone)

ledger.note: 1308: the Northern Sakhalin Ainu are subdued. 'Waying and Yushannu' offered surrender through the Nivkh and promised a yearly tribute of furs: 'With this, the war between the Ainu and the Mongols was over' (Sakhalin page); the Ainu page: 'by 1308 had been subdued'. No annexation: the Ainu 'paid tribute to the Yuan dynasty at posts in Wuliehe, Nanghar, and Boluohe', so the land stays Ainu with a tributary tie.

region.text: the coast and offshore islands of Taizhou in Zhejiang, where Fang Guozhen took to the sea (the place is the fang-guozhen-s-regime dossier's reading; this page does not name it)

ledger.note: 1348: Fang Guozhen, accused of piracy, flees to sea and holds the Zhejiang coast outside Yuan control. P2: 'Accused in 1348, he fled to sea.' The page gives the year but not the place, so the region is the other dossier's reading (confidence 1). P2 also says 'He surrendered to the Yuan in 1356' and 'In 1367 he surrendered to Zhu Yuanzhang'; the land stays in his dossier throughout and is not drawn as a Yuan vassal, to avoid two colours on one coast.

region.text: the city of Qishui in southern Hubei (about 115.25 E, 30.45 N), seat of the Tianwan regime

ledger.note: September 1351: Zou Pusheng takes Qishui and enthrones Xu Shouhui as emperor of the Tianwan, the first lasting rebel state of the Red Turban Rebellions. P2: 'In September, Zou captured the city of Qishui in southern Hubei and enthroned Xu Shouhui as emperor.' The radius is the researcher's. Also P1: 'Red Turban Rebellion led by Song loyalists started and grew into a nationwide uprising' (1351).

region.text: Hanyang, Hankou and Wuchang, the three cities of modern Wuhan

ledger.note: 1352: the Tianwan holds the Wuhan cities. P2: the new state 'briefly held Hanyang, Hankou, and Wuchang before being driven off in 1352'. The page dates only the driving-off (1352), not the taking, which may fall late in 1351; 1352 is placed as the year the cities leave the Yuan, and the same year's gain below returns them. The tianwan dossier's ledger/4 keeps this loss in 1353 and should move it to 1352.

region.text: Jiujiang, Nanchang and Changsha on the middle Yangtze, Gan and Xiang

ledger.note: 1352-1353: Tianwan forces advance to Jiujiang and take Nanchang and Changsha. P2 is silent on all three cities; the date and places are the tianwan dossier's, read there from the Tianwan page, which this run did not open. A gap-filler should open it.

region.text: Hanyang, Hankou and Wuchang, the three cities of modern Wuhan

ledger.note: 1352: the Wuhan cities leave the Tianwan. P2: the new state 'briefly held Hanyang, Hankou, and Wuchang before being driven off in 1352' (the page names no one as the driver; the Yuan armies are the page's general force in 1352-1353; confidence 2). Ni Wenjun retakes Hanyang in 1356 (ledger). The tianwan dossier's ledger/4 dates the Yuan's retaking to 1353 and should move to 1352.

region.text: the Tianwan capital Qishui and the Jiangxi and Xiang cities (Jiujiang, Nanchang, Changsha), recovered by Toqto'a's army; the Wuhan cities are the separate 1352 gain

ledger.note: 1353: the Yuan army under Toqto'a retakes the Tianwan land. P2: the Yuan armies 'suppress most of the Red Turbans by 1353'; the page lists none of these places (Qishui, Jiujiang, Nanchang, Changsha) and the capital Qishui falling 'by fall' 1353 is the tianwan dossier's reading of the Tianwan page, not P2's. The Wuhan cities are not in this event: P2 dates their loss to 1352 ('driven off in 1352'), and they are the 1352 gain above (repaired 2026-10-25; the first draft had them here, with the wrong note that the page lists no places). P2 also dates Toqto'a's personal recovery of Xuzhou to October 1353 (no rebel state; not a territorial event here).

region.text: the city of Gaoyou on the Grand Canal in northern Jiangsu

ledger.note: 1353: Zhang Shicheng seizes Gaoyou, the base of his later state. P2: 'By the end of 1353, Zhang had taken the city of Gaoyou.' The zhang-shicheng-s-wu dossier dates its founding to 1354 (Zhou page), when Zhang declared the state; the loss is entered at the page's date. P2 does not date Zhang's capture of Yangzhou.

region.text: Bozhou in western Anhui, where Han Lin'er was proclaimed emperor, and the Yingzhou district to its south (the second circle is the han-song dossier's reading; P2 names Bozhou)

ledger.note: 16 March 1355: Han Lin'er is proclaimed emperor of a restored Song at Bozhou. P2: 'He was proclaimed emperor on 16 March 1355 at Bozhou.' The page dates the Song's proclamation, not the Yuan's loss of the district, which it does not date (confidence 2). P1 puts the renewed Song loyalist dynasty in 1351 'with its capital at Kaifeng', which P2's Bozhou (1355) and Kaifeng campaign (1358) contradict; P2 has Han Lin'er drowned in January 1367.

region.text: Changshu, Suzhou, Changzhou and Huzhou in the lower Yangtze and Taihu region

ledger.note: 1356: Zhang Shide's army takes Changshu (February), Suzhou (March) and pushes west and south into northern Zhejiang. P2 does not date any of these ('does not date a siege of Suzhou in 1356'); the dates and places are the zhang-shicheng-s-wu dossier's, read there from the Zhang Shicheng and Zhou pages, which this run did not open.

region.text: Hanyang, retaken by Ni Wenjun, who 'moved the capital there'

ledger.note: 1356: Ni Wenjun retakes Hanyang and moves the Tianwan capital there. P2: 'Ni retook Hanyang and moved the capital there' in 1356 (after succeeding Zou in 1355). The tianwan dossier dates the retaking to January 1355 from the Tianwan page; P2 says 1356.

region.text: Huguang (Hubei and Hunan), held by Tianwan and then by Chen Youliang

ledger.note: 1356: Tianwan holds Huguang. P2 dates no territory beyond Hanyang for the Tianwan; the region and year are the tianwan dossier's (Tianwan page, not opened here). Chen Youliang, who replaced Ni Wenjun in 1357, proclaimed the Han in 1360 (P2). Confidence 1: a bridge to the Cliopatria-based 1363 shape, which this dossier cuts in Hubei and Hunan.

region.text: the north-eastern provinces of Korea, the Ssangseong Prefecture

ledger.note: 1356: King Gongmin's army retakes the northern provinces from the Yuan. P5: 'In 1356, the Goryeo army retook these provinces partly thanks to the defection of' a minor official and his son Yi Sŏng-gye; the provinces named are the Ssangseong and Dongnyeong Prefectures. The goryeo dossier has Dongnyeong back in 1290 (Goryeo page) and only Ssangseong (Hamgyong) in 1356; the two pages disagree on Dongnyeong, and the region here is Ssangseong only.

region.text: the Kingdom of Goryeo, no longer a tributary

ledger.note: 1356: Gongmin cuts the ties with the Yuan. P5: his first reform was removing pro-Mongol aristocrats and officers and he cut ties with the Yuan; the page gives no year for the reforms, and the year of the break is that of the retaking of the northern provinces (confidence 2). P5 also mentions a deposed pro-Mongol faction hoping to renew ties with the Mongols (undated) and Red Turban invasions of Goryeo in 1359 and 1361.

union.text: Qingyuan (Ningbo), where Fang held de facto control
Shaoxing, under Fang's de facto control

region.text: Qingyuan (Ningbo), Taizhou, Wenzhou and de facto Shaoxing, Fang Guozhen's ports (the fang-guozhen-s-regime dossier's region)

ledger.note: By 1356 (bridging): Fang holds the Zhejiang ports. 'By 1356, Fang permanently controlled three coastal prefectures in Zhejiang, Qingyuan, Taizhou, and Wenzhou' with de facto control over Ningbo and Shaoxing (undated); the page gives no year of the conquest, only this upper bound. After 1356 the Yuan named him Duke of Qu, a nominal tie not drawn as vassalage (see notes). The 1348 loss above is the first circle on this coast; the Taizhou circle here overlaps it.

region.text: Jiqing, renamed Yingtian (Nanjing), and its district, taken by Zhu Yuanzhang

ledger.note: 10 April 1356: Zhu Yuanzhang takes Nanjing, the base of the future Ming. P2: 'He took Nanjing on 10 April 1356.' Zhu had joined the Red Turbans under Guo Zixing on 15 April 1352 (P2). The radius, less Zhang Shicheng's Gaoyou zone, follows the zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu dossier.

region.text: Jiangxi, held by Chen Youliang's forces

ledger.note: 1357: Chen Youliang, who replaced Ni Wenjun in 1357 (P2), holds Jiangxi; P2 says only that he was 'ejected from Jiangxi in 1361'. The year of the acquisition is the tianwan dossier's (Tianwan page, not opened here).

region.text: Sichuan without Kham, and Chongqing, taken by Ming Yuzhen in Xu Shouhui's name

ledger.note: 1357: Ming Yuzhen takes Sichuan for the Tianwan. P2 says nothing about when Ming Xia arose ('does not date the founding of Ming Xia'); it says Ming Yuzhen died in 1366 and his son surrendered in 1371. The year and the vassal link (the ming-xia dossier takes the title 'king of Longshu' in 1360) are the tianwan and ming-xia dossiers', not P2's.

region.text: Shandong, where Mao Gui ran the Song government's province

ledger.note: 1357: the Song government's Shandong province. P2 does not mention Shandong; the year is the han-song dossier's bridge ('between 1356 and 1359 the Song government set up five provinces'). P2: in 1357 Zhang Shicheng accepted Yuan titles (no territorial event).

region.text: Putian, seized by the Ispah army

ledger.note: 1357 (bridging): Putian. 'The rebel army seized control of Quanzhou, Putian, and even reached the provincial capital Fuzhou' without dating Putian or Fuzhou; placed in the first year of the rising, as the ispah-rebellion dossier does.

region.text: Quanzhou, Putian and the approach to Fuzhou, which the Ispah army 'even reached'

ledger.note: 1357 (bridging): the Yuan side fights the Ispah army for Putian and the approach to Fuzhou. The page dates only the seizure of Quanzhou (March 1357) and the end (1366); Fuzhou is where the rebels 'even reached', not a city they held. Mirrors ispah-rebellion ledger/1.

region.text: Quanzhou, seized by the Ispah army in March 1357

ledger.note: March 1357: 'Sayf ad-Din and Amir ad-Din, the commanders of the Ispah army, seized the opportunity to control Quanzhou' (Ispah rebellion page; infobox 1357-1366, Fujian). The army was raised by the Persian Shi'a Muslims of Quanzhou; the Yuan lose the port city and its hinterland to a rebel state that the Yuan's own Fujian commanders fight for nine years.

region.text: inland Zhejiang, the Jinhua and Quzhou uplands

ledger.note: 1358: Zhu Yuanzhang holds four inland Zhejiang prefectures. P2 gives no date; the year and the circle are the zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu dossier's.

region.text: Ü-Tsang, the Sakya lamas' government under the Yuan

ledger.note: 1358: the Sakya regime's rule over Tibet ends and the tint ends with it. P4: 'Tai Situ Changchub Gyaltsen superseded Sakya in the period 1354-1358, thereby recreating an autonomous Tibetan state'; the Phagmodrupa dynasty is dated 'Established: 1354'. 'Toghon Temur was beset by inner troubles, and so preferred to confirm the acquisitions of Changchub Gyaltsen, and conferred the titles darakache and tai situ' (undated). Repaired 2026-10-25: the first draft also carried a 1358 'loss' of Ü-Tsang to tibet, but this dossier never holds Ü-Tsang directly (the 1294 and 1352 corrections cut it and /2 draws it as the sakya-regime's vassal land), so there is no Yuan land to lose; the true mirror of tibet's 1358 gain is the sakya-regime dossier's 1358 loss to tibet. The tibet dossier's ledger/0 and /1 still name yuan-dynasty and should name sakya-regime.

region.text: Kaifeng, the former Song capital, and the Henan plain round it

ledger.note: 11 June 1358: the Red Turban Song's Kaifeng campaign begins. P2: 'The Kaifeng campaign began on 11 June 1358.' (P1 has the renewed Song of 1351 'with its capital at Kaifeng'.)

region.text: Kaifeng

ledger.note: June 1358: Liu Futong's army takes Kaifeng. P2 dates only the start of the campaign (11 June 1358) and the retreat (10 September 1359) and does not say the city was taken; the capture is the han-song dossier's, read from the Han Lin'er / Song page.

region.text: the Bozhou and Yingzhou district, retaken from the Song by Chaghan Temür

ledger.note: 1359: Chaghan Temür drives the Song back from Bozhou and Yingzhou to Anfeng. P2 says only that Chaghan Temür won a string of victories from 1352 and was assassinated in 1362; the year of the retaking is the han-song dossier's.

region.text: south-western Jiangsu round Nanjing and Zhenjiang, and Anhui south of the Yangtze

ledger.note: By 1360: Zhu Yuanzhang holds the south bank of the Yangtze round Nanjing and southern Anhui. P2 gives no date for these; the year is the zhu-yuanzhang-s-wu dossier's bridge.

region.text: Kaifeng

ledger.note: 10 September 1359: the Song retreat from Kaifeng. P2: 'the retreat came on 10 September 1359'. The page does not say the Yuan reoccupied the city.

region.text: Kaifeng and its plain

ledger.note: 10 September 1359: the fighting over Kaifeng ends with the Song retreat (P2).

region.text: Shandong

ledger.note: 1362: the Song provinces other than Jiangnan are gone. P2 does not mention Shandong; the year is the han-song dossier's bridge.

region.text: Hangzhou, the Song capital, less the inland Zhejiang circle Zhu Yuanzhang held

ledger.note: 1363: Zhang Shicheng takes Hangzhou and declares himself Prince of Wu. P2 (paraphrased): in 1363 he took Hangzhou and declared himself Prince of Wu. P2 dates the siege of Suzhou, where his Wu ends, from 27 December 1366 to 1 October 1367.

region.text: northern Jiangsu, which Zhang 'occupied' after refusing the Yuan offer

ledger.note: 1363: northern Jiangsu. P2 is silent; the year and region are the zhang-shicheng-s-wu dossier's bridge (Zhou page, not opened here).

region.text: Quanzhou, Putian and the approach to Fuzhou, which the Ispah army 'even reached'

ledger.note: 1366: 'it was eventually crushed by the ethnic Han commander Chen Youding' (loyal to the Yuan); the infobox gives a Yuan victory. The Ispah army had 'collapsed into internal conflict' in 1362. Mirrors ispah-rebellion ledger/4.

region.text: Quanzhou and Putian, the cities the Ispah army seized in Fujian

ledger.note: 1366: Chen Youding crushes the Ispah army and Quanzhou and Putian return to the Yuan. The page gives 1366 and the Yuan victory but does not say in words that the cities were recovered ('imperial soldiers killed most of the Semu merchants in Quanzhou'); the land returned is read from the seized cities, as the ispah-rebellion dossier reads it (its ledger/5). Fujian stays Yuan to 1368 under Chen Youding.

region.text: the North China plain: Henan, Hebei, Beijing and Tianjin

ledger.note: 26 April 1368: the first dated clash between the new Ming and the Yuan army. P2: Köke Temür 'was dismissed in February 1368, and the Ming defeated him on 26 April'; Zhu Yuanzhang had proclaimed the Ming on 12 January 1368 at Yingtian (P2). The page does not place the battle; the zone is the researcher's reading from Xu Da's march from Kaifeng to Tongzhou.

region.text: Henan, where Kaifeng lay

ledger.note: By 15 August 1368: Henan is Ming ground. P2: 'Xu Da led an army north from Kaifeng' on 15 August 1368, so the Ming held Kaifeng by then; the page does not date the capture. Köke Temür was dismissed in February and defeated by the Ming on 26 April 1368, and the warlord Li Siqi surrendered on 21 May 1369 (P2); the page does not place either.

region.text: Khanbaliq (Dadu) and its hinterland, Hebei, Beijing and Tianjin

ledger.note: 14 September 1368: Dadu falls and the Yuan court leaves China. P1 infobox: 'Fall of Dadu: 14 September 1368'; 'He fled north to Shangdu from Khanbaliq (present-day Beijing) in 1368 after the approach of the forces of the Ming dynasty'. P2 gives Xu Da's march (15 August), Tongzhou on 10 September and Khanbaliq on 14 September in one passage and 20 September in another; the Zhizheng era table on P3 ends 10 September 1368. Shangdu fell on 20 July 1369 (P2).

region.text: the North China plain

ledger.note: September 1368: the fighting for the North China plain ends with the fall of Dadu. The Ming-Yuan war goes on in Inner Mongolia and the north-west under the Northern Yuan (northern-yuan dossier, contest from 1370).

region.text: the Mongolian Plateau, where the Genghisid court retreated

ledger.note: September 1368: the court retreats to the steppe and continues as the Northern Yuan. P1: 'In 1368, following the defeat of the Yuan forces by the Ming dynasty, the Genghisid rulers retreated to the Mongolian Plateau'; the infobox gives 'Formation of Northern Yuan dynasty: 1368-1388' and the text says the rump lasted to 1635. Toghon Temür dies at Yingchang on 23 May 1370 (P2). The northern-yuan dossier begins in September 1368 and asks this one to end the Chinese Yuan in 1368 and not to draw the Mongolian core in 1368-1374.

region.text: Yunnan, held by Basalawarmi, Prince of Liang

ledger.note: Yunnan holds out for the Yuan. P1: the resistance of the Prince of Liang Basalawarmi 'in Yunnan and Guizhou was defeated in 1381'. The page does not say when the province was cut off; 1368 is the principality-of-liang-yunnan dossier's date (Basalawarmi page, not opened here).

region.text: the Yuan realm as drawn for 1363-1367 (with the Bozhou-Yingzhou district and, after the 1366 gain, Quanzhou and Putian), less the Ming conquests recorded above

ledger.note: 14 September 1368: the Yuan dynasty ends with the fall of Dadu. P1 infobox: 'Fall of Dadu: 14 September 1368'. The land goes to the Ming (China), the Northern Yuan (Mongolia) and the Liang principality (Yunnan); the Phagmodrupa had taken central Tibet in 1354-1358 and Goryeo its north in 1356. The Ming took Shangdu on 20 July 1369 and received the surrender of Ming Xia's Sichuan in 1371 (P2), and Yunnan held out to 1381 (P1), so the successor handovers are staggered; the Cliopatria Ming row begins in 1375.

wars.name: Red Turban Rebellions

zones.text: Hubei and Hunan: the Tianwan 1351, Chen Youliang's Han 1360-1364
the lower Yangtze: Zhang Shicheng's Wu, Zhu Yuanzhang's Wu, 1353-1367
Sichuan and Chongqing: Ming Yuzhen's Xia

wars.outcome: The Yuan loses the south to rebel states, and Zhu Yuanzhang, a former Red Turban commander, crushes his rivals one by one (Chen Youliang killed at Poyang Lake in 1363, Zhang Shicheng at Suzhou on 1 October 1367, Fang Guozhen's surrender in 1367) and proclaims the Ming on 12 January 1368 at Yingtian; the Ming take Dadu on 14 September 1368.
wars.note: P2 infobox 1351-1368. Toqto'a was dismissed in January 1355 on P2 (P1 says 1354). The Yuan page: 'Red Turban Rebellion led by Song loyalists started and grew into a nationwide uprising'; in 1354 Toghon Temür dismissed Toghtogha and relied on local warlords. The Yuan warlords Chaghan Temür (assassinated 1362), Köke Temür (named 1361, succeeded 1362, dismissed February 1368), Bolad Temür (seized the capital 1364, assassinated August 1365) and Li Siqi (surrendered 21 May 1369) fought each other as much as the rebels (P2; the 1366-67 civil war of the warlords is undated there).

wars.name: Ming northern campaign of 1368

zones.text: Henan, Hebei, Beijing and Tianjin: Xu Da's march from Kaifeng, 15 August 1368, to Tongzhou, 10 September, and Dadu, 14 September

wars.outcome: Ming victory: Dadu falls on 14 September 1368, Toghon Temür flees to Shangdu (taken 20 July 1369) and then Karakorum, and the Yuan rump continues as the Northern Yuan.
wars.note: Not a named article. P2 has no section for the campaign and the dates above are its passages on the Ming advance. The first clash is Köke Temür's defeat on 26 April 1368. The fighting continues in the northern-yuan dossier (Yingchang seized after Toghon Temür's death on 23 May 1370).

wars.name: War of the Two Capitals
wars.outcome: 'Khanbaliq-based Tugh Temür eventually won the civil war against Ragibagh known as the War of the Two Capitals.' A succession war inside the Yuan (Shangdu against Khanbaliq); no land changed hands.
wars.note: Listed so the reviewer sees it was considered. Ragibagh was supported by Yesün Temür's retainer Dawlat Shah; Tugh Temür later 'mainly a puppet of the powerful official El Temür' (P1). The reigns around it are in P3.

wars.name: Kaidu-Kublai war, Yuan phase (Yuan and the western khanates)

zones.text: the Altai and western Mongolia between Karakorum and the Dzungarian steppe (the ogedeid-ulus dossier's zone)

wars.outcome: Inconclusive (infobox 1268-1301). Kaidu 'refused to submit to Kublai and threatened the western frontier'; Duwa raided the Yuan from 1298; Kaidu beat Khayishan's force in 1300 and died in 1301 'after the battle near Karakorum'. 'A peace later came in 1304 which established the nominal suzerainty of the Yuan Emperors over the western khanates', though 'their subservience was nominal and each continued its own separate development' (P1). No land is recorded as changing hands.
wars.note: Repaired 2026-10-25 from the Kaidu-Kublai war page. The war ends in 1301 (the page's infobox and Kaidu's death); the peace of 1304 with Duwa's Chagatai Khanate (the western khans' recognition, P1) is in the outcome, not the span. The belligerents are the Yuan, Kaidu's House of Ogedei and Duwa's Chagatai Khanate. Partial disagreement with the reviewer: the infobox lists the Ilkhanate and the Golden Horde ('1284 after') on the Yuan's side, not against it, and describes no fighting by either against Kaidu in 1294-1301; they are left out of the list because they drew no zone here and the list does not carry sides, not because the page keeps them out of the war. Cliopatria's three allegiance rows (Chagatai Khanate 1294-1374, Golden Horde 1294-1362, Ilkhanate 1294-1343) are not drawn as vassalage: see notes. The contest events mirror ogedeid-ulus ledger/8 and /9.

wars.name: Second Mongol invasion of Burma

zones.text: Singu and Male, the southernmost Mongol garrisons, about 70 km from Tagaung (the myinsaing-kingdom dossier's circle)

wars.outcome: Failure for the Yuan. The Myinsaing brothers seized the Mongol garrisons at Singu and Male in January 1300; the Mongol army reached Myinsaing on 25 January 1301 and withdrew on 6 April 1301 for a bribe; the Yuan abolished the province of Zhengmian and left northern Burma entirely on 4 April 1303.
wars.note: The Myinsaing page calls 1300-01 the second Mongol invasion (infobox 'Last Mongol invasion: 1300-01'); the war entry runs to 1303 to include the evacuation of Zhengmian (First Mongol invasion of Burma page: 4 April 1303), which is the ledger's 1303 loss. The first invasion (1277-1287) is in the mongol-empire, pagan-kingdom and myinsaing dossiers. Mirrors myinsaing-kingdom ledger/1 and /2.

wars.name: Ispah rebellion

zones.text: Quanzhou, Putian and the approach to Fuzhou, which the Ispah army 'even reached'

wars.outcome: Yuan victory (infobox 1357-1366, Fujian). The Ispah army seized Quanzhou in March 1357, took Putian and reached Fuzhou, collapsed into internal conflict in 1362 and was crushed in 1366 by the Han commander Chen Youding, loyal to the Yuan.
wars.note: A Fujian rising inside the Red Turban years, not part of the Red Turban Rebellions page's story; the Yuan side was Chen Youding and Toghon Temur's government. Mirrors ispah-rebellion ledger/1, /2, /4 and /5. Fujian is the Yuan's in the 1363 correction except Quanzhou and Putian.

wars.name: Mongol campaigns against the Ainu (Mongol invasions of Sakhalin, Yuan phase)

zones.text: northern Sakhalin, where the Northern Sakhalin Ainu fought the Mongols (the ainu dossier's zone)

wars.outcome: Mongol victory (infobox 1264-1308): in 1308 the Northern Sakhalin Ainu surrendered and promised a yearly tribute of furs, 'the war between the Ainu and the Mongols was over'. No annexation: the Ainu paid tribute at Yuan posts (Wuliehe, Nanghar, Boluohe).
wars.note: The war began on 30 November 1264 (mongol-empire dossier); this entry covers the years under the Yuan row. The page dates one Ainu raid on the mainland beaten near Lake Kizi in mid-1297 and one more raid in 1305 that evaded the Mongol army, and describes the Mongol presence as tributary and trade-based, so northern Sakhalin is a contested zone, not Yuan land; the zone is the ainu dossier's reading and the contest events mirror its ledger/3 and /4.

certainty.note: The steppe, Siberian, Tarim and Tibetan frontiers are approximate; the provincial frontiers of China follow the Branch Secretariats of P1 but no survey line is given; Korea's frontier follows the goryeo dossier's outline.
The front lines between the Yuan and the rebel states moved with each campaign and are drawn by province or by city radius; none is a surveyed line.

sources.title: Yuan dynasty
sources.note: Identity, 1271-1368, Dadu and Shangdu, the 11 M km2 area of 1310, Tibet's Bureau, Goryeo's tribute, the western khans in 1304, Red Turbans, the fall of Dadu on 14 September 1368, the Northern Yuan and the Yunnan holdout to 1381. The page has no section headings and no list of provinces.

sources.title: Red Turban Rebellions
sources.note: Dated events 1348-1370: Qishui, Gaoyou, Bozhou, Nanjing, Hangzhou, Kaifeng, Köke Temür, Xu Da's march and the fall of Khanbaliq. The page is silent on Ming Xia's founding, Sichuan, Shandong and the 1366-67 warlord war. Reread 2026-10-25 for the Wuhan sentence: 'The new state expanded southward and briefly held Hanyang, Hankou, and Wuchang before being driven off in 1352.' The page does not mention Jiujiang, Nanchang or Changsha, and says nothing of Yuan control of Bozhou or Yingzhou after 1359.

sources.title: List of Yuan emperors
sources.note: Reigns for the ruler strip (era dates; Ragibagh, Kusala and Irinjibal are the researcher's mapping of the Chinese entries).

sources.title: Phagmodrupa dynasty
sources.note: Sakya rule 'on behalf of the Mongols', superseded 1354-1358, the Yuan as 'overlord of Tibet', Ming titles from 1372; silent on Kham, Amdo and 1368.

sources.title: Gongmin of Goryeo
sources.note: The retaking of the northern provinces in 1356 and the cutting of ties with the Yuan (undated); the Red Turban invasions of 1359 and 1361. Silent on Hamgyong by name, on the Yalu forts and on the Ming era.

sources.title: Ispah rebellion
sources.note: Infobox 1357-1366, Fujian, Yuan victory. 'In March 1357 ... the commanders of the Ispah army, seized the opportunity to control Quanzhou'; 'seized control of Quanzhou, Putian, and even reached the provincial capital Fuzhou' (Putian and Fuzhou undated); 'In 1362, the Ispah army collapsed into internal conflict'; 'In 1366, it was eventually crushed by the ethnic Han commander Chen Youding' (loyal to the Yuan). The page does not say in words that Quanzhou returned to the Yuan; the infobox result is a Yuan victory.

sources.title: First Mongol invasion of Burma
sources.note: Infobox 'Northern Burma to Tagaung added to the Yuan dynasty'; 'The Mongols continued to occupy northern Burma to Tagaung as the province of Zhengmian (Cheng-Mien)'; 'on 4 April 1303, the Mongols abolished the province of Zhengmian (Cheng-Mien)', evacuated Tagaung and returned to Yunnan. Silent on who took the land afterwards and on the year Zhengmian was set up.

sources.title: Myinsaing Kingdom
sources.note: 'In January 1300, the Burmese army led by Athinkhaya seized lightly manned southernmost Mongol garrisons' at Singu and Male, 'only 70 km from Tagaung'; the Mongol army 'managed to reach Myinsaing on 25 January 1301' and called off the attack for a bribe on 6 April 1301; the Mongols 'withdrew from northern Burma entirely on 4 April 1303'; 'In the north, the brothers took over Tagaung but could not go any farther north' (undated, after the withdrawal). The page calls 1300-01 the second Mongol invasion.

sources.title: Fang Guozhen
sources.note: 'Fang created a pirate band in 1348'; 'By 1356, Fang permanently controlled three coastal prefectures in Zhejiang, Qingyuan, Taizhou, and Wenzhou' (how and when he took them is not given); de facto control over Ningbo and Shaoxing (undated); the Yuan made him Duke of Qu 'after 1356'; surrender to Zhu Yuanzhang in December (1367 by inference).

sources.title: Kaidu–Kublai war
sources.note: Infobox 1268-1301, inconclusive. Kaidu's side: Chagatai Khanate, House of Ogedei, Golden Horde (until 1284); the Yuan side: Mongol Empire (1268-1270), Yuan dynasty (1271-1301), Ilkhanate, Golden Horde ('1284 after'). 'From 1298 on Duwa increased his raids on the Yuan'; 'in 1300, Kaidu defeated Khayishan's force'; Kaidu 'died in 1301 after the battle near Karakorum'; 'a peace later came in 1304 which established the nominal suzerainty of the Yuan Emperors'. The page does not name western Mongolia.

sources.title: Mongol invasions of Sakhalin
sources.note: Infobox 1264-1308, Mongol victory, 'Ainu people in Sakhalin become tributaries of the Yuan dynasty'. The Mongols attacked on 30 November 1264; armies crossed in 1285-1286; an Ainu raid on the mainland was beaten near Lake Kizi in mid-1297; one more Ainu raid in 1305 evaded the Mongol army; in 1308 Waying and Yushannu surrendered and promised a yearly tribute of furs: 'the war between the Ainu and the Mongols was over'. The page does not say the Yuan held or annexed northern Sakhalin; the only Mongol fort it names is Shiranushi at the southern tip.

sources.title: Ainu people
sources.note: 'The Northern Sakhalin Ainu resisted the Mongols, but by 1308 had been subdued'; they paid tribute at Yuan posts; no annexation is stated. Second page for the 1308 contest end.

sources.title: Kaidu-Kublai war
sources.note: fx-26 (F191, F193): 'the Yuan was forced to start withdrawing from Kashgar, Khotan and Beshbalik' in 1288/89 (Beshbalik military colony of 1286, garrison under Qi Gongzhi since 1280); the Altai fighting 1293-1301 (Kaidu defeats Khayishan 1300, Kaidu dies after the 1301 attack on Karakorum); a peace of 1304 'established the nominal suzerainty of the Yuan Emperors' over the western khanates.

sources.title: Kaidu
sources.note: fx-26 (F193): Kublai 'ensconced his forces at Beshbaliq from 1278' and set up postal stations and military colonies in Uighuria; 'Kaidu and Duwa were able to take over Beshbaliq in 1286, forcing Kublai's troops to evacuate Uighuria' over the following years; Duwa became Chagatai khan in 1282; Kaidu captured Karakorum in 1289.

sources.title: Kingdom of Qocho
sources.note: fx-26 (F191): vassal of the Mongols from 1209 to 1335 (infobox), 'allied with the Yuan against the Chagatai Khanate' and made Prince of Gaochang in 1308; later 'became part of the Chagatai Khanate' (no year given); last known ruler 1352; gone by the 1370s.

sources.title: Hongwu Emperor
sources.note: Opened 2026-11-01 (fx-38, H12). Dated Ming gains from the Yuan: Taiyuan January 1369, Shaanxi by September 1369, Shangdu/Yingchang 1370, Sichuan September 1371, Gansu 1372 (Feng Sheng), Yunnan 1381-1382, Manchuria 1387-88. Silent on Ningxia, Guizhou and Hainan (1374).

notes:
YUAN DYNASTY (ea-06-a). Five pages opened (page budget for 3 shapes: 1-2; three more were opened because the 1363 shape drops Korea, Tibet and the south, and no border move may stand unexplained): Yuan dynasty, Red Turban Rebellions, List of Yuan emperors, Phagmodrupa dynasty, Gongmin of Goryeo. Each Wikipedia fetch returned a model-written digest of the page, not the page text; sentences in quotation marks are the digest's quotations and a gap-filler should check the wording against the page.

DATES. The state is drawn 1294-1368. (a) Start: the Yuan name was proclaimed in 1271 (P1: 5 November 1271) and the Song conquest ended in 1279, but Cliopatria's Mongol Empire row runs to 1293 and its Yuan row begins in 1294; the mongol-empire dossier owns 1271-1293 (rename, Song, Dai Viet, Champa, Burma, Goryeo) and hands its land to this one. The mongol-empire dossier dates the rename 18 December 1271 and P1 says 5 November 1271 (disagreement). (b) End: Cliopatria runs the Yuan to 1374. P1 and P2 date the fall of Dadu to 14 September 1368 (P2 has 20 September in another passage). The Northern Yuan dossier begins in September 1368, calls the Cliopatria row's 1369-1374 years wrong (the land is Ming China and the Mongolian core) and asks this dossier to end the Chinese Yuan in 1368. Done: yuan-dynasty_1363 is adjusted and bounded to 1368; Cliopatria's 1369-1374 is not drawn from it.

SHAPES. Cliopatria's three shapes (14.25, 14.25 and 12.2 M km2) differ little before 1363 and draw all China, Korea (South Korea 99 percent, North Korea 99.6 percent), Xizang (99 percent), Mongolia, a quarter of Russia and 35 percent of Xinjiang as direct land. Corrected: Goryeo and Ü-Tsang become vassal tints (ledger 1294, ends 1356 and 1358); the 1363 shape drops nine rebel provinces. Areas from the gazetteer at the shape's own scale: 13.3 M km2 (corrected 1294), 10.9 M km2 (corrected 1363). P1's infobox: 11.0 M km2 for 1310 (ratio 0.77 against Cliopatria, 0.83 against the corrected shape).

JUDGEMENTS A REVIEWER MAY WANT TO OVERRULE. (1) Tibet as a vassal tint: P1 says the Bureau of Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs 'governed Tibet'; P4 says the Sakya ruled 'on behalf of the Mongols' under the Yuan as 'overlord of Tibet'. A province would be direct land; the sakya-regime dossier is a separate state, so the tint is used (confidence 1; the start 1264 is that dossier's). (2) The three Cliopatria allegiance rows (Chagatai 1294-1374, Golden Horde 1294-1362, Ilkhanate 1294-1343, each 16-19 M km2 as a relation shape) are NOT recorded as vassalage. P1: the supremacy of the Yuan emperors 'was recognized by the western khans in 1304', but 'their subservience was nominal and each continued its own separate development', and only the Ilkhans 'truly recognized Kublai as Great Khan'. Drawing three empires in the Yuan's lighter tint would be false; the wars list carries the relation. (3) Annam, Burma and Champa 'recognized Mongol hegemony and established tributary relations' (P1, no years; Temür Khan 'made peace with' Vietnam, which paid tribute 'for a few decades'): not recorded, no dates. The invasions are in the mongol-empire, ngo-dynasty, champa and pagan-kingdom dossiers. (4) Rebel states the Yuan accepted back (Fang Guozhen 'surrendered to the Yuan in 1356', Zhang Shicheng 'accepted Yuan titles' in 1357, P2) are not drawn as Yuan vassals; the land stays in the rebel dossier.
